title: I built those ethical constraints first, and then I started exploring what AI could do.
author: Lance Eaton
summary: In this interview with Kirsten Davis—Professor of Law at Stetson University and 2026 recipient of the Legal Writing Institute's Mary Lawrence Innovation Award—Lance Eaton explores how a law professor navigates AI in legal education. Davis uses AI daily in both instrumental ways (research, finding information in her files via Copilot) and exploratory ways (experimenting to understand how students might use these tools and what is good or bad about that use). Her organizing concept is "sustained critical engagement": designing assignments that keep students deeply interacting with course material rather than using AI to bypass that engagement. She distinguishes "learning to write" from "writing to learn" and focuses her AI experiments on the latter—using AI to improve the quality and depth of feedback she gives students rather than to reduce her own effort. Her most striking finding is that using AI in a three-way dynamic (original text, her own thinking, AI-generated options) is cognitively richer than the two-way dynamic of just reading and responding, making feedback work more intellectually engaging rather than less. The interview surfaces a model for ethical AI adoption: building explicit constraints first, then exploring capability within those boundaries.
points: Sustained critical engagement is the organizing principle: assignments must require students to genuinely interact with course material, not use AI to bypass that engagement

AI can improve the quality and depth of feedback without reducing the teacher's intellectual engagement—the three-way dynamic between original text, the teacher's thinking, and AI options is more cognitively rich, not less
Ethical AI adoption starts by building constraints first: Kirsten Davis established her ethical framework before exploring what AI could do, which kept exploration anchored to educational values
quotes: About the Interview series As part of my work in this space, I seek to highlight the folks I’ve been in conversation with or learning from over the last few years as we navigate teaching and learning in the age of AI.
If you have experiences around AI and education in higher education classrooms that you would like to share, consider being interviewed for this Substack.
Kirsten Davis is a Professor of Law at Stetson University College of Law in Gulfport, Florida.
Davis has studied legal communication, education, and ethics for two-and-a-half decades.
She recently served as the Provost's Faculty Fellow for Generative Artificial Intelligence and Higher Education at Stetson.
Her current research focuses on the ways in which generative artificial intelligence impacts legal writers and readers.
She founded the Legal Writing and Generative AI Convo Group, an online monthly forum for law faculty interested in generative AI and legal communication.
She is the 2026 recipient of the Association of American Law Schools Section on Legal Writing, Reasoning, and Research Section Award and the Legal Writing Institute’s Mary Lawrence Innovation Award.
